title: Moses Blesses the Tribes of Israel
summary: Before his death Moses pronounces a blessing over Israel. He opens by describing the LORD coming from Sinai with his holy ones and becoming King over his people, then speaks a word over each tribe in turn: Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph, Zebulun and Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher. He closes by praising the incomparable God of Jeshurun, whose everlasting arms hold Israel, and declaring Israel blessed as a people saved by the LORD.
story: Moses has charged Joshua, handed over the law, and sung a song warning of Israel's coming unfaithfulness. Now, as a father on his deathbed, he blesses his people. The scene deliberately echoes Genesis 49, where Jacob, the father of the twelve tribes, gathered his sons and spoke over each one before he died. Where the Song of Moses in chapter 32 looked ahead with warning, this chapter looks ahead with hope. It is Moses' last spoken word in the Bible. Chapter 34 will narrate his death and pass the leadership fully to Joshua, who will bring the tribes into the lands this blessing anticipates.
historical:
The chapter presents itself as Moses' blessing before his death, set on the plains of Moab. Like the Song of Moses, the poem contains archaic Hebrew forms, and many scholars regard it as an old composition, though its date is debated. Some tribal descriptions seem to assume life already settled in the land: Zebulun and Issachar calling peoples to a mountain and drawing wealth from the seas (verses 18-19), and Dan leaping from Bashan in the far north (verse 22), where the tribe later moved according to Judges 18. Those who hold to Mosaic authorship read these as prophetic; others see them as reflecting the tribes' later situation.

The chapter's list of tribes also carries history. Simeon is not mentioned. In Joshua 19:1-9 Simeon's territory lies within Judah's, and the tribe seems to have been absorbed into Judah early on, which may explain the omission. Levi, which received no territory, is blessed instead for its priestly role. Joseph is treated as the father of two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh (verse 17), which together formed the heart of the later northern kingdom.
cultural:
In the ancient world a father's final blessing was not a pleasant wish but a weighty and, in Israel's view, effective word. Isaac's blessing of Jacob (Genesis 27) and Jacob's blessings of his sons and grandsons (Genesis 48-49) shaped the future of whole families. Moses, called here “the man of God” (verse 1), a title used for prophets, blesses Israel as a father would. The blessing is prayer and prophecy at once.

Several details reflect Israel's institutions. The Urim and Thummim (verse 8) were objects kept by the high priest, probably in the breastpiece he wore (Exodus 28:30), and used to seek God's decision in difficult matters; exactly how they worked is not known. Levi's willingness to disregard family (verse 9) recalls the Levites rallying to Moses after the golden calf and acting even against their own relatives (Exodus 32:26-29). The Levites' duties are summed up as teaching God's law and offering incense and sacrifice (verse 10). The blessing of Joseph lingers on agricultural abundance (dew, deep waters, sun, seasons, hills) because in a land dependent on rain rather than river floods, the fertility of the soil was a direct gift of God. Asher dipping its foot in oil speaks of rich olive country.
literary: The chapter has a frame and a center. The opening hymn (verses 2-5) and the closing hymn (verses 26-29) praise the LORD as King and Protector of Israel, and they surround the tribal blessings (verses 6-25). The frame keeps the focus on God: whatever each tribe receives, it receives from the one who came from Sinai and rides the heavens. The tribal sayings vary widely in length and style. Reuben's is a single verse; Joseph's is the longest and richest. Many use animal imagery (Gad a lion, Dan a lion's cub, Joseph a firstborn bull and wild ox), which also features in Jacob's blessing in Genesis 49. The closing beatitude, “Blessed are you, O Israel,” gathers all the tribes back into one people.

outline.t: Introduction: the blessing of the man of God
The LORD comes from Sinai and becomes King
None like the God of Jeshurun

doctrines.note: The LORD became King in Jeshurun when the tribes gathered (verse 5). Long before Israel had a human king, God was its King, and the blessing of each tribe flows from his rule.

The eternal God is Israel's dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms (verse 27). The chapter portrays God as both shelter above and support beneath, caring for every tribe in its own place.
Israel's blessing is summed up in being a people saved by the LORD (verse 29). Their security rests not on their strength but on the God who shields and fights for them.

words.note: Berakah, blessing. In the Old Testament a blessing is a spoken word that conveys God's favor, fruitfulness, and life. The chapter begins by calling itself the blessing Moses pronounced, linking it to the patriarchal blessings of Genesis and to God's original blessing of humanity in Genesis 1:28.

Meonah, dwelling place or refuge, sometimes used of an animal's den. The eternal God is your dwelling place (verse 27). Psalm 90, titled a prayer of Moses, opens with a closely related word, calling the Lord his people's dwelling place in all generations.

Yasha, to save or deliver, the root behind the names Joshua and Jesus. Israel is a people saved by the LORD (verse 29). Salvation here means rescue and security from enemies, the concrete deliverance Israel knew from the exodus onward.

Jeshurun, a poetic name for Israel meaning something like the upright one. In chapter 32 it was used ironically of Israel growing fat and rebellious; here it frames the blessing with honor (verses 5 and 26), showing how God still names his people by what he intends them to be.

christ: The chapter's closing words, “Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD?” (verse 29), use the same root as the name Joshua and the name Jesus. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one through whom God's people are finally saved and blessed. Judah's blessing (verse 7), a prayer that the LORD would help Judah against its foes, is brief, but other Scripture develops Judah as the royal tribe from which David and his greater Son would come (Genesis 49:10). The priestly blessing on Levi, who teaches God's law and offers sacrifice, finds its fulfillment, according to Hebrews, in Christ as the great high priest. And Moses' description of God as King among his people anticipates the kingdom Jesus proclaimed. These links are drawn by later Scripture; the chapter itself is a blessing for Israel's tribes as they prepare to enter the land.
questions: Moses ends his life by blessing rather than warning. What difference does it make to be blessed by someone at an important moment in your life?
The eternal God is described as a dwelling place with everlasting arms beneath. When have you needed to know that you were held from below?
Each tribe receives a different blessing. How might God's care for his people look different in different lives, while still coming from the same God?
